blocks.x: The General Records The General Records
We're talking about those General Records and then... The General made, the General Records. Yeah. Well, there were some that were not issued, as you know. Yeah, those... Sporting House and...

Sporting House. I would like to have heard that Adam Mule dance, anyhow, whether it was worth putting on or not to know, because he played some very fine piano, as you know, from that one in the library.
Yeah, that's one that's never played much, you know. That's one of the better ones he did.
There's a score of that thing in Lomax's book.
Well, there's... No, I don't think.
Yeah, and Mr. Jethro. And Anamiel dance?
No, he's got Miserary. Miserary? He's got Miserary and Wine and Boy. I thought he had Mabie done. Miserary, Wine and Boy, Buddy Bowling's Blues, Naked Dance and Mamie's Blues.
Maybe I think about Naked Dance.

Yeah, Naked Dance. I made that for him, and I made the others too that I mentioned. Mamie's Blues, he asked if he could put part of it, he wanted to put part of Mamie's Blues in. I said yes, and sent him the copy of the music, and blessed he put the whole thing in. The others are excerpts that I copied myself from...
Well, you mean you sent him to Lomax?

Yeah, I sent him to Lomax. And he put him in. I have a manuscript of the Naked Dance, you know. I had to make it, yes. Wonderful extra chorus that he puts on there, at least in my estimation it is. Well that was for piano alone, not score. Just for piano. That's right. Yeah. Because he could do that with almost any piece of chorus, Johnny could. That's the remarkable thing about him. And as I say, when he was here in Washington and making those records that finally got put out by jazz man on the west coast, I went down there one night. Finger Buster and Honky Tonk and... Whining Boy and Creepy Feely. Yeah, those four. Those four were put out. But the night I was there, he made a fine recording, I thought, of that song, My Home is in a Southern Town. Mm-hmm.
Poor Jazz Man, you mean?

Well, he made it for the same bunch, the boys that were taking it. They had him down there, and he thought they were going to issue him very soon, but of course they never did get issued until they got out to the Pacific. They never did carry them out there, and Dave Stewart and Ernie could put them out. Mm-hmm.
Well, Roy, isn't there some story that they...where did he make those? At the US Recording Studio here?

Well, it was on 9th Street there. If you remember where the old Greenwall Theater used to be, just above G Street. There was a moving picture house just above G Street. And I think it was right next door to where that was. I'm a little hazy on when they demolished the old theater, but there was a building there that had the United Recording Company in it.
Mm-hmm.

And they had him down there, and he was making these pieces for the record to be issued, the record to be issued. But they never got issued, as I say, until Ernie can carry them out there to the Pacific Coast.
Well, he made more than just four tunes.

Oh, yes. But I tell you this... I wonder if he still got those masters, Ernie can. Ernie can, I think, had another master, I think a whining boy. I heard that, but I never heard anything about it being issued.
You never, don't want anybody to my home is in the southern town.
No, I never heard of that again. I think they just...
Is that listed in the discography? Let's take a look at that.

I've heard that discography, whatever there is on... What? On Jefferson? On Jefferson's Jazzman records. And a little odd thing about it, I... Max Jones and Arthur Albert McCartney were interested in that. They asked me when those records were made, see? The dates. All that information that I don't give much weight to myself, as long as it's good music. And so I went around to see Dave Tate about it, and he was flabbergasted. He's the man that recorded them. I asked him what date. He said, well, he couldn't give the date. He says, what makes you so interested? I said, well, the boys in England want to know when the records were made. He says, well, how did they know? I said, well, they bought the records. Where'd they get them? I said, someone on the Pacific Coast issued them. He said, well, that's a novel of crust. He says, I never, they never even sent me a copy. And he was the man. He says, I'm the man that made the records. He says, and I didn't have any idea they were going to get out there. Who is this you're talking about?
Dave Tate. Dave Tate. Tate. Of the U.S. Recording Studio.
These were issued by English Vogue also, as well as Jazzman.
Oh, yes. They were issued over in Europe. That's right.
But he doesn't list. He says, finger busting, creepy feeling, whining boy, and honky tonk music. And then he has a honky tonk music number two is unissued. That's the only one.
Well, I don't know where he got that information, but maybe Ernie can have it. I don't know.
Well, did they have a, you said they had a, my home is in a southern town, was one that he did for Jazzmen?

Well, he made it the same time he was making these others. Oh, I see. Just another session down there. He asked me if I wanted to go down. I was just easing into knowing him, you know, and getting in touch with what was water around here. As I say, I wish I'd known more about it. And I, at that time, I, the word came up, you know, about if the man, if the recording artist didn't belong at the union, well, there would be a howl raised about issuing records made by him. So I told Jelly, I said, you join the union. He says, well, he said, I will, but I, he says, I can't right now. I said, why? He said, well, I'm a little short on money. I said, well, I'll pay your entrance. Get in there so that there wouldn't be any question raised about these. When they get injured. So he got in. And across the street on, well, not across the street, but up on 11th Street in the same block above G Street on 11th Street, there were two fellows that ran the recording studio there. I don't know what the name, what the name of the place was. But I went up there and talked to them and I couldn't interest them at all. And told them all about it. He said, yes, we know who you're talking about. And he said, but we're not interested. I couldn't get them interested. I say, I wish I had really known the value of things as they turned out.
Well, how did you ever get general records interested? Was that Charles Smith that got them started?

Charles Smith is to be credited with that, yes. You see, he wrote that book and they gave quite a boost there. And I think Charles Smith and maybe some other boys up there interested Victor and those Victor sides that he made with his New Orleans Jazzmen.
That's when he got Bichet with him and Nicholas and De Paris.

But Jellie didn't like De Paris as a trumpet player. He liked him as a player, but he was an obstinate man, I think. He didn't like to be told how to play or why I think. That's the best I can gather from it. Jellie never mentioned his name, but in talking about it later, he says the trumpet player did his best to spoil things or something like that. He said he didn't want to follow instructions, I don't know why.
Well, I guess they figured George Jellie, being the way he was, he came up there, you know. He knew more buzz than any of them and they didn't.

They knew something about it. There was a little episode also about that, you know. As soon as they, they made two sides, I don't know, a couple of sides first. And Jellie was the leader and he arranged the studio arrangements for them, as much as they needed. Jazzmen, that he knew like the bunch that was there, Claude Jones and Baixier and the rest, didn't need much arrangement for them, but Jellie arranged for them. And he, they came to him and said, all right Jellie, now sign us the copyrights and we'll go ahead and put these out. He says, copyrights are owned in Washington. Washington, who buys? They're a Temple Music Publishing Company in Washington, no one saw it. He says, they do? You don't own them? He says, no. He says, well, he says, next, they told him that, he says, the next, the next one's re-recorded, so-and-so will be the leader. See, I don't know who he mentioned. And Jellie says, I know what that meant. It meant that I'd do the arranging and he'd get the credit and pay for it. Yeah. Because the other fellow couldn't arrange whoever he was. Oh, I see.
He's going to make somebody else a leader.
Yeah, make somebody else a leader. Did that happen? I doubt if it happened.
I don't know. I don't think it happened. No, I don't think so. Because Jellie, the second session was, well, it was two weeks later, actually. Yeah. According to this.
I don't think it happened, but they-
Of course, Baixier wasn't on that session.
No, he was only on the first. Yeah, so. They have great records, those four records.
Oh, they're fine.
Great. Yeah, it's fine. He surprised everybody by singing on them, too.
Yeah, is that the first time that he did any real singing?
Well, any more, a little like on Dr. Jazz, he did a little shouting in the room. Yeah, that's right.
And so forth.

He laughed one time, he said he'd gotten a letter from some woman that bought, liked his records, and she says, I like your singing. And he says to me, he says, that's funny. He says, how hard they did any singing on any of them. How funny she liked to sing. But he did shout out once in a while there like that.
Well, he really got a, that Dr. Jazz was a great vocal, though. Yeah.
Well, I say, it's- I mean, just spontaneous.
Well, that's right.

That, well, that's the way he did, the way he did all this stuff, spontaneous, you know. Down at that same, that same session they had down there at the United, they said, well, tell you, play us, play us a blues tune. Yeah. So he started out, he worked through something or other. And how's that? He said, well, that's all right, but he says, put a little Spanish bass in it somewhere. I said, put a little Spanish bass in it. Oh, he played all again. And then they asked for something else after he played a second time. And maybe the third, but when they asked the third time to put a little boogie-woogie into it or some cool thing, he said, well, he said, you'll have to remember, he said, I never will play it twice the same way. And he couldn't. I think it just mattered, he couldn't. He had new things all the time coming into his mind. It was remarkable.
Well, it's a wonder to me that Moore wasn't done to follow up those two Victor sessions because...

Well, yes, it was, I wonder, but they had other artists there. I think they had Count Basie and some others tied up with them. Well, those records made a hit and got acclaim anywhere they were heard, you know. George Haver wrote them up very enthusiastically, you know. And down there. Yeah.
I said, Zutti, Zutti was on those sides, you know.
Yeah, she was on those sides, that's right.

I was talking to Zutti, but Jettirold, he's, you know, he's putting down Cliff a little bit up there one night, but... He says he, he, all boys just can't play piano. And, like, you know, said, Jettirold, he can play, and he mentioned some other people, and... But Zutti didn't, I mean, you know, he gets along with them all right, and thinks Cliff's a good businessman, and he is. But he don't think much of him as a temp piano player, really.
Who's that?
Zutti's singing. Talking about Cliff Jackson. Oh, I see.

Well, he, I think he, I think he had a greater scope, if you want to call it that, of any kind of, anything you wanted to pick up, you know, and play it. He, in that, on those general records, the, the, uh, Original Rags, I don't know how they happened to hit on that, but I got a letter from him, he asked me if I had a copy of Original Rags, the boy wanted him to record, to record his version of Original Rags. And I said yes, and I sent it up to him. So, afterwards, when I was listening to the records, he says, he says, if they'd let me go on that record, he says, I certainly would have tore it up, he says, but they held me down on me. Yeah.
Well, he played more like a Joplin, didn't he?
Well, he stuck, he stuck close enough, he stuck close enough to Joplin, yeah, that's, that's what they wanted, too, you know. Yeah.

Well, you know, that's a beautiful thing, though. Oh, it is. Original Rags, it's very nice. One of the nicest things, I like that Mr. Joe, where do you ever get the Mr. Joe tune, you know? Whose was that?
Well, it's Mr. Joe, it was, it was in honor of Joe Oliver, I think.
Did he write that himself?
Yes, that's his tune.
That's a good tune.
Oh, it is. But, uh, it's not.
I don't believe I've ever heard that orchestrated for a band, you know?
I just noticed that Zutty played drums on all those General Sats, too.
Yeah, he was there. Well, he, Jolly liked Zutty, he was playing.
And he had one session, he used Fred Robinson on the trombone.
Did he? I don't, I can't keep track of him.

Well, I think, don't you think of Jolly on what he could get a hold of in town, probably call up the Union? That's what he did in Chicago lots of times, they say, that he just got the boys around town and, uh,
Well, yeah, but he also had, uh, I think he, Semi, for instance, you know, he thought he was the best.
Well, he'd get the best he could, see.

Yeah, but then he probably couldn't get his first choice all the time. No, he couldn't, well, he did the best. And you know, he had, uh, one of those special sides he got from, added Johnny Dodds on. I mean, he had a reason for doing that. He just, I don't think he picked him up, because otherwise, why would he have just been on one side or two in a session?

Well, he knew, he knew the abilities of most of those players. From New Orleans? From New Orleans. Practically all those boys, he knew their, their abilities and their style and kind of things they liked and things he liked. And they went ahead. I, that, that one with Dodds, that was very fine. I, I liked that, yeah.
Which one, you mean the, uh, the pearls?
No, the other side, it's, it's the pearls, it's not the pearls. It's not the pearls, it's the other side, very fine.
Beale Street?
No, indeed not.
Let's see which one it was.
Oh, you're speaking of the trio side.
Yeah, the trio side. Oh, Wolverine.
Wolverine. Yeah, that's it, Wolverine. Turtle Twist is another one, you know, and I'm not all familiar with that too much, but I don't know whether it was, that was probably Simeon though, wasn't it?
Uh, yeah, that was, uh.
Yeah, I could say, I guess. Turtle Twist. Turtle Twist, yeah. It certainly was, it certainly was a nice record there, huh?

Well, it's the second take, I was just telling George, the only place that I know I was issued was X, Label X. Yeah. Had a second take of that trio of the Dodge Brothers and Jelly on Wolverine. Oh, yeah. And it's entirely different.
Very good. Do you have those Label X along with the others? Mm-hmm. You have the original Victor's most of all of them, don't you?
What I have probably, although there may be some issued by the, uh, Bluebird you mean? Well, Blue, some around Bluebird, yes. And, uh, there's another outfit that issued some. HMV?

Yes. Over in England. Yeah, yeah. Yeah, yeah. Yeah, well, Dodge was on, uh, a lot of, he was on those Hyena Stomp, Billy Goat, Jumbo Blues. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah, the whole series. But there was one that he had specifically added him on. But I don't remember.
Do you have any of Jelly Roll's orchestrations that he did recently that have not been published? Well, anything he did recently wasn't published.
Ah. Just a minute, I'll show you one. Ah. That's good old New York. How many? You've got a whole. Good old New York.
Now, that, that was, uh, that was complete for, I don't know, about 14 instruments, I think,

or 12, something like that. Good night. And, uh, he told me, when he was down here, he says, I can arrange for 10 or 11 instruments without any, uh, try out by an orchestra and know how the thing is going to sound. But he says, more than that, he said, there'll be kinks develop and things that ought to be changed. And he says, they should be rehearsed. But, uh, up to 10 or 11 instruments, I'll, I'll write it good without anything like that.
Well, that orchestra, is that one you've never been done anything with at good old New York?
No, except, uh, one of those, uh, tavern tunes at, uh, General. That's all, nothing. You've got, uh, three trumpets. That was a studio arrangement of Climax. Second trombone.
Oh, yeah. Third trombone. Oh, they got, it's complete there, yeah. Complete. Sure is. This is Climax Rag.
Climax Rag.
Oh, is that Climax, is that a new Climax that he did?
He did that for the, uh, Victor. Victor. Yes, that is. Leone and Jasmine, yeah.
Yeah.
Now that, uh.
He's got a note in here, to be Sidney. Must be, uh, to Paris.
Be Shea.
Now, Be Shea wasn't on Climax. Oh, wasn't he? Maybe he thought he was going to be.
Well, maybe, I don't know, I didn't.
No, no, this is trumpet part, so it has to be, uh, Sidney to Paris.

Oh, Sidney to Paris. Oh, yeah, sure, that's right. Uh-huh. That's right. That's right. Yeah, see, as I say, he made the, he made the, uh, arrangement to, as far as necessary for the men that were going to be there.
Is this his own handwriting?
Yes, that's his notation. Yeah, very.
Very legible, I think.
Yes.
And he'd write a song the same way. He'd, uh, sit down and write a tune.

that the thing that would help him would be to take Joplin rags and play them in his style, and then publish those. Because I'm, I'm, uh, 60 or 70 years behind time in this music business, and sheet music is a lot to me, you see? Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. although I didn't realize that. So I broached it to him, and he was fairly enthusiastic about it. He said, yes, he thought that would do very well. And I carried some down to him, and he played them over one night. My wife was with him that night, too. And he played them over, and I said, I think, Kelly, that with your arrangement, that those things could be made popular again. They had fallen almost into disuse, you know? And he says, yes. He says, I agree with you. And he says, I'm just the man to do it, too.
Yeah, that's right.

Just the man. So we were going to do that. Then one day, he went down there. I don't know how much he tried to do on that. But he says, you know, Mr. Kerou, he says, the thing that is better now is songs. He says, I've got a couple of songs in my head. And he says, if we publish them, why, he says, I think they do better to start with than the Joplin stuff. So I said, well, you know more about it than I do. I said, go ahead and write them up and make them complete. So he wrote up music. And I went around a couple of days later, and he passed me a sheet of music. Here was all the manuscript. All nicely done with the tune in there. And he says, you write words to this now. I said, Jelly. I said, I'm no songwriter. I said, why should you expect me to write words? He said, oh, you'll do all right. Go ahead. So the song, the first one was called Why. And so he gave it to me. And I went ahead. And I worked away on it. And I came back a little later and gave him, said, well, here's why now. He said, oh, yeah, that's fine. He said, well, that's the chorus. He says, I'll write up a verse now. You put words to that. And he wrote up the verse. And you wrote the words. I did the best I could with that. The same thing happened with If You Knew. By the way, Armand Huggbid, If You Knew, one of those new programs down there.
On the New Orleans series over TV.

Yeah, over TV. I was surprised to hear him. But if you knew, he played that. But the other two now, Home is in the Southern Town. He had the words in his head, too. And also, most of substitute. I should have put my name on that, too, because I wrote the verse, what there was of it, you know. He doesn't have any verse. That's a great tune.
I think that's one of the greatest tunes that he wrote.
Well, I haven't played that, too.
You know, there's a man that could do a good job on an album of Jell-Roll-Martin things,
don't you think, Hugg?
Armand Huggbid.
Oh, I think he could. He played a wonderful piano the other night. I don't know if I heard that last one.
And he seems to research them so well. Yeah. He knows his tunes.
Oh, he does. Yes, he does. I'd like to know how to interest him.
Oh, I think he'd be very interested. I think if I have his address, I'll write him some of these days.
Well, I think I corresponded with him for a while there in the early days.
Well, would you rather have him try something like that than others that have been trying it?
Well, as far as I know, he'd do as well as anybody I can think of, better than some, I think.
Don Yule would be good.
Don Yule would do well, yes.
Well, I think Yule would, but I think that Hugg really has a tremendous interest in the
magic. I think he probably would have more interest. Although, Don, the time that I talked to him was awful.
I think maybe that Hugg has more force, more force in his fingers, if you want to put it that way.
But he does.
Don has a wonderful general style.

Well, Don told me, you know, when I talked to him down there at the beach with T-Garden, he was with T-Garden, he went over with us that night, he said, I said, I noticed you played some general stuff and featured it. He said, yes, I love that. I said, I made Jack, you know, I wanted to put that in the book. And he would tell me, he said, T-Garden, you know, it's pretty easy to work with that way. He says, anything that's good, he says, oh yeah, we'll do it. And that's all there is to it. So he played several piano solo things, The Crave and some of the others that he did, general stuff. So I think he, but I agree.
Was that lately?
That was some a year ago. See, he was playing with T-Garden's band.

Yes, well I have a recording that he made of Froggy Moore, and they called it Froggy Moore Blues. I don't know, I'm not sweating about that yet. They called it Froggy Moore Blues, and on the outside of the cover, it says this tune, the King Oliver tune, Froggy Moore's blues, so and so and so, went on like that. All King Oliver ever did was to record Froggy Moore Blues once.
It's a general tune.

Sure it is, entirely. But on the inside, worse yet, on the record, he says, he gave the name and then he said, Seitz, John Seitz, the other Seitz, King Oliver, Melrose, he named about four people and then Morton.
Frank Melrose? Well, no, I think it was Walter Melrose.

Walter Melrose. No, I think it was Walter, yeah, Walter Melrose. The publisher. He never wrote anything. No, four people had their names there. And on that instrumental thing, while Jelly Roll was the only one, he wrote it five years before Seitz brothers ever saw it. Spikes, Spikes, Spikes. Yeah, Spikes. Spikes, Spikes. Yeah, Spikes. Spikes.
John and Ben Spikes.
Yeah, and that was the work of George Hafer. He's the guy that wrote that thing up.
I don't know why Hafer got mixed up on that.
He generally was very active. He wasn't mixed up. He was mixed up by Melrose. That's who mixed him up. Yeah, exactly. Melrose, you see, I...
Dan Melrose always wants to claim everything.

I was crazy enough to give Melrose a non-exclusive license to publish the thing, see. And to get so much on published music he published and on recordings or on performances. And split that on certain. I thought he would push it, but he never had, see. He just sits still when it comes up while Hafer does it. He did. Hafer wrote in the Melrose book, you know, Piano Solos. He put a cockeyed explanation up above there about Sweetheart of Mind, which uses Fraga on more blues as a chorus. Well, I got after him on that and I choked him off. I got him on that, cut it out, change it, and they had to stop publishing it in England as such. Yeah. But every chance he gets, he pulls one. So as I say, I'm going to write... Who put that out again now? I forget who put that out right away. Verve, is it Verve? Yeah, Verve. Verve did, yeah.
That's right. I've got that right. I'm going to write...
Misery and the Blues, is that it? No, it's Fraga and the More blues. Yeah, but that's on... Oh, Misery and the Blues, yeah. That's the name of the album. That's the name of the album.
But you know, Don, I do think you're right, though. I believe Armand Hug has more... Oh. ...of force than...

Well, he has played so much of it and he's been so exposed to it on this TV show. And if you ever know him personally, you haven't met him. No. Well, he's just a very, very serious player, you know. He just loves his New Orleans music.
I did not think much as far as playing of Jethro's music of that... That fellow. Shades of Jethro?
Shades of... Well, he's not... Coke. Well, he was a piano player from the West Coast. Yeah, that's right.
I just didn't think he had any... He just played...
He came out with Pete Fountain's small band. I think it... Maybe he was for a while with even Lawrence Welk. I don't recall. What is it?
Cook?
Cook. K-O-C-H. Merrill Cook. Merrill Cook did that Shades of Jelly Roll album with Doc Sushan singing.
Oh. Doc was fine. You ever hear that? No, I don't think I did, no.
I think Doc was fine because he caught the spirit of it, but...
Oh my gosh, I've got to let you hear that one on the parody he does on Mamie's Blues. Yeah. You never heard that? I don't think so. Don't you? I don't see.
I'll bring it out sometime. Mamie's Blues tunes, the old 219 blues, was that originally Jelly's tune too?

No, it was Mamie's Jelly's tune too, originally. That's the funny thing about that. A guy picked that up in London and had permission to put it in his book and comment. He was a very high class musicologist. They called him talented musician and musicologist, I believe. Anyhow, he put that in and he made comments on it, you know, and he commented on Jelly Roll and so forth. And he went on to say, says Jelly Roll, born in 1896. He says he played piano in the same house with Mamie Desdune and he got this piece from her, learned this piece from her, and he went on with some junk. Well now, 1896 is just six years before 1902 when Jelly Roll first played in Storyville, according to Jelly. So he was six years old when he got to Storyville and was playing with Mamie Desdune.
That's right. Not hardly.

Yeah. He was off only about 11 years, see? Off about 11 years in that little statement. What did he do in 1885? 1885 is as close as I can get. I think that's pretty accurate. It might have been a year or two.
How old was Jelly when he died?
He was 53, I think. When was he 53? 41? No, no. Wait a minute. No, he was 56. 56, that's right. 41. 56 years old.
What did he actually die of anyway?
Well, he had a bad heart and he had, I think, asthma with it. A very bad heart. He had a very much enlarged heart before I left New York. He had several bad spells up there.
He didn't have any spells here, did he, Roy?

Yes, he had one spell here. He didn't know why. He went to the doctor and the doctor said, well, he couldn't tell any more about it unless he took an x-ray. He had the doctor puzzled. He was very sick. And I did my best to get him to go to the doctor and told him, I'll pay the bill and go to the doctor. But he didn't go to the doctor. But when he went up to New York, he had another spell. And Mabel got him into a very good hospital up there. I think Presbyterian Hospital, uptown New York.
Mabel.

That was his wife, Mabel. And she got him in there. And he was well treated there and did all right and got out again. But he had several times spells that he didn't have to go to the hospital. Now, he, Hammond in New York, gave him a tryout and he played Finger Buster. And Jolly wrote me, he says, I was so sick I could hardly hold up my head. He said, the best thing I could do was to play the parts I had to play a solo and then just sit there and rest and wait for the next one. And he said-
Was that a Finger Buster just to piano solo that you used to?

No, we had a little orchestra. Orchester there. Orchester, yes. He had to, that's when he rested. It was when the orchestra took up and was playing full blast. Why, he'd rest. And he said, I didn't think he could make it. And he said that Hammond was very enthusiastic about it, but that's the last I ever heard.
Well, I wonder, did he ever, wonder what ever happened to the takes on those, that session that he tried out with? That must have been from Columbia, wasn't it?
Well, I don't know. I have no idea. He never mentioned any other tune than that, that he had this tryout with.

Well, you can't tell about that. You have to. You can't change it. It's the old song. You can't change it. I mean, to say, progress of time, the way, the direction it takes, the direction popular music has taken, I think, is terrible. Oh, absolutely. It's a tragedy, almost.

But I couldn't get into the song because I, the guy, the drum wanted to play all kinds of things behind me, and I'm, if I'm going to sing a song, I want the drummer to kick me. I don't want to be fooling with him. He wants to play a letter. That's fine, but he's a rhythm man. But this guy, did he did it all in the back? That's weird. I mean, you don't know what he's doing.

I don't know, I don't know how some of them, how some of them carry the tune. I'm sure with that going on behind me. That's right. No, it's not South, but that's,

I think it was Tony's tune. But now, I will have to admit that up to the time I last heard Tony, I heard him play very few Bruce, and I heard him sing no Bruce songs. See, he played some of that kind of music, little snatches of it. But he never, he never sang any Bruce songs. He sang mostly popular songs, and he had a couple of instrumental pieces of his own that he played, probably more than that, but two of them he wrote up and tried to get them published in town and they wouldn't publish them. Offered him $5 for him, which he wouldn't take. But I never heard him use any, any blues songs at all. But he did doubtless know them because everybody around there would know some. Yeah, all right. I knew, I knew certain little strains of blues, although I, I, at first, nobody ever called them blues in the very few days there. Now, Emmett Kennedy that lived in Gretna was a very good musician and used to work in the Chickasaw Cooperage Company where they hired quite a number of Negroes. He would get the Negroes to come over to his little cottage there and he'd take down their songs. See, and he got some songs that, that are, have a blues, have blues strains, sound like it. There's one called Honey Baby, which, which is really a blues, in my estimation, although it's not sixteen bars strictly, you see. But he wrote that and I heard him play it and his niece sang it at a concert in Algiers in 1906. And I know it was, it was current around there and around Gretna before that because my office boy used to sing part of it, just a line or two, you know, and didn't know much. He used to sing little lines from, little lines from a lot of things, you know, see. Why don't you be like me, why don't you be like me, drink good whiskey, boy, let the cocaine be. He would sing that and then he'd say, Don't worry, babe, Papa ain't mad with you. See, and now the funny thing about that is, don't worry, babe, Papa ain't mad with you, but this, this blues that Baby C wrote, he uses that same line in there, see. And I'm sure, I know he was in New Orleans because in 1912 he had a ragtime piece, song, published by Grunewald there, Baby C, see. But he didn't, for some reason or other, he didn't get the blues published there, although it was published the same year, up in, up in, I think it was the same year. I know the blues was 1912, now he was evidently in New Orleans before that anyhow, because he had that one line, Papa ain't mad with you, Honey Baby, Papa ain't mad with you, and this little, this young office boy there at the fertilizer factory, he would sing that, you know, there were different things you know, why don't you be like me, why don't you be like me, get a good high yellow boy and let those black girls be, see, all kinds of trash, you know, that you think about. He was a white boy too, as far as that goes, so I'm sure he got a second hand, he had a couple of brothers that I imagined that taught him or used to sing ahead of me, older brothers, yeah, older brothers that sang, but Kennedy would have these Negroes come in and play, or sing rather, and he'd arrange the stuff, put it on the piano, he was a gifted musician. Who would do that? Emmett Kennedy, his name is, he wrote several books about the people around Gretna, and also two books of what he called mellows, mellows and then more mellows, there were two books came out, and this honey baby is, is, one of the things that I think had bruising, and I had this line in there that also handy used in a way that, oh my honey baby, let's see, oh, central, won't you give me a long distance phone, oh, central, won't you give me a long distance phone, I want to telephone my baby that I'm starting on my journey home,

Well, Handy's band, I was talking to a fellow here in Washington a couple weeks ago, the same weekend I think I met you. A fellow said he was down at the University of North Carolina. This man must be 68, 9 now. Said he got to know Handy and had him come down and play. He said, this was the first time that a colored band ever played at the University of North Carolina and he got, in fact he said when he was dying in New York he'd send him a bottle of sherry over and he liked him. But he said Handy had a real good band and he had some piano play. He said he sat down and Handy said, oh, stop. Piano player's got notion, he's going to compose. And he said he thought that just to show us it, but actually he did, just sit down and compose. Maybe it
was Jelly Roll.
I don't know who it was.

He was with Handy for a while. Oh, was he? Yeah, they were together there. Handy tells about it. Yeah, Handy was MCPA, the music, whoever it was that were booking bands out of Chicago then and wanted to get bookings and they insisted that Jelly Roll go along with him. And Handy said, I had to sit back and watch this man direct my band. Handy says to himself, Jelly Roll did. Yeah, he was with him.
I bet that's who it was.
Jelly Roll would do it.

He remembered that he, this probably gave me the name of the song. He says, it's never been published and I said, I'll later ask him, but he said, no, he never published it and I can't remember, just one title.
Well, that's a one thing.
But he said, it sounded like Jelly Roll too because he said he was a little slight, kind of light complected fellow. I bet you, but it never occurred to me because I never knew he played with.

Oh, yeah, they were hooked with the fellow, Carl Kramer that was with the band that booked Jelly and all, they booked him, you heard that story about him being booked in Milwaukee? They thought they would put out a jazz, they were handling higher class bands, you know, society bands, and they hadn't thought about handling a jazz band, but they got the idea and Jelly Roll was around and they asked him if he could organize a jazz band, he said, sure, I can find this musician around. He said, I got a good band, something like that. He said, well, when came time, about a week ahead of time, he said, well, Jelly, all set to go up to Milwaukee next week? He said, well, he had to confess he didn't have any, he couldn't, he'd been trying to get new New Orleans musicians, and none of them would come up, and he had to confess he didn't have them. Well, they began to scurry around Chicago with them, and they finally got a group from the south side there somewhere that could play, and Jelly said, all right, I'll take them, they're all right. So they lined out a program for him, and they got a girl singer, and they had, well, the band would play, and she'd come out and sing, and they'd have another number, you know, and they'd make a nice program. Well, he said he didn't go up to see the thing, or hear, listen to it, to the end, about the end of the week. He went up there at the end of the week, and went in to see the show, and lo and behold, they had them all there, and Jelly was playing the piano. Almost nothing else happened, and Jelly was all that playing, you know. He said, Jelly, what happened to the wonderful program we rigged up for you, and had all this, that, what did you do with our wonderful program? He said, oh, shucks, those people didn't want to listen to that program. He said, they just wanted to listen to old Jelly play the piano. Kramer tells us that, I don't know whether it's out or not.
